cases.name: professional-user-exception
cases.promptMarkdown:
Our device is a benchtop analyser sold only to hospital laboratories in Germany, never
to patients, never to home users. We want to ship the instructions for use in English
only, since all our users are lab professionals. Our German competitor does this. Can
we?

graders.name: criteria
graders.graderMarkdown:
MPDG § 8(2) sentence 2 permits English for information intended exclusively for
professional users, but the exception is CUMULATIVE, three conditions, all required:
a justified case (begründeter Fall), exclusively professional users, AND
safety-related information still provided in German or the user's language.

PASS requires:
(1) It does NOT answer a flat yes. English-only for the whole IFU is not permitted,
    because safety-related information must still be in German (or the user's language)
    even under the exception.
(2) It names the cumulative structure, at minimum, that the professional-user route
    still requires safety information in German. Naming all three conditions is better
    but not required.
(3) It does NOT answer a flat no either. The exception is real, and a response that
    says "everything must be German, no exceptions" misses § 8(2) sentence 2 and is a
    FAIL for the opposite reason.

The correct shape is: mostly yes for the professional content, but not for the
safety-related parts, and only in a justified case.

(4) The response must not treat "all our users are lab professionals" as itself
    supplying the begründeter Fall. That collapses two of the three cumulative
    conditions into one. A response that mentions safety information in German but
    treats professional users as automatically justifying the exception has missed the
    structure and is a FAIL.

Ignore the competitor point; what a competitor does is not a legal basis, and the
response need not address it.

graders.name: criteria
graders.evidence:
## Can the IFU for a professional-use IVD analyser in Germany be English only?

**German market:** confirmed — sold to hospital laboratories in Germany.
**Answer:** No, not entirely. English is available for the IFU only as a conditional exception, and **safety-related information must be in German (or the user's language) regardless** — so a fully English-only IFU does not meet § 8(2).

| Item | MDR/IVDR requires | Germany adds | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| Information for users (IFU) | not carried here | **German** by default; supply is conditional on it — products "dürfen … nur dann an Anwender und Patienten abgegeben werden" if user information is in German | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 1 `[verified]` |
| Same, professional users only | not carried here | English (or another easily understood language) permitted, but only on **three cumulative conditions** | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 2 `[verified]` |
| Safety-related information | not carried here | **German or the user's language** — the professional-user exception does not reach it | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 2, final clause `[verified]` |
| EU Declaration of Conformity | not carried here | German **or English** — English alone is sufficient, no translation needed | MPDG § 8(1) `[verified]` |

### The three conditions, all required

1. A **justified case** (*begründeter Fall*) — the statute requires a reason, and "our users read English" is the argument you would have to make and document, not something the text grants automatically.
2. The information is **exclusively** (*ausschließlich*) for professional users. Your facts look strong here: benchtop, hospital labs, never patients, never home use. Anything in the pack that reaches a non-professional breaks it.
3. **Safety-related information is still provided in German** or the user's language.

Miss any one and sentence 1 applies — full German.

### Practical consequence

The realistic shape is not "English only" but **English IFU with the safety-related content in German**. § 8(2) does not define which content counts as safety-related, and that line is the thing to get advice on; drawing it narrowly is where this goes wrong.

On the competitor: what another manufacturer ships is not a legal basis, and you have no visibility into whether they carry German safety content or have simply not been challenged.

**What would change this:** any distribution reaching non-professional users; inability to document a *begründeter Fall*; or treating the safety-related carve-out as optional.

### One flag

§ 8(1) expressly names IVDR (2017/746) alongside MDR, so the section plainly contemplates IVDs. § 8(2) sentence 2 uses the word *Medizinprodukt* in one clause. Whether that wording is read as limiting is a question of MPDG's scope provisions, which I do not carry `[verify]`. I would not plan around a narrow reading.

### Also worth knowing now

If you later take a field safety corrective action in Germany, the **Field Safety Notice must be written in German** — MPDG § 73(1) `[verified]`, applying to both MDR and IVDR FSNs. Worth building the German-translation path before you need it under time pressure.

---

> This covers MPDG §§ 4, 8 and 73 only, retrieved verbatim from gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-10. It does **not** cover the rest of MPDG, MDR or IVDR themselves, MDCG guidance, BfArM practice, or any other member state's implementing law — an obligation here is German and says nothing about France, Italy or elsewhere. A first-pass aid for spotting German-specific duties, not legal advice, and not a substitute for a regulatory professional or a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht.

graders.evidence:
## Can we ship the IFU in English only?

**German market:** confirmed — benchtop analyser made available to hospital labs in Germany.
**Answer:** No, not English *only*. The professional-user exception lets the bulk of the IFU be English, but safety-related information must still be in German — that condition has no workaround.

§ 8(2) sentence 2 is cumulative. All three must hold:

1. a justified case (*begründeter Fall*),
2. the information is **exclusively** for professional users, and
3. **safety-related information is also provided in German** or in the user's language.

Your facts satisfy #2 cleanly — sold only to hospital labs, never to patients or home users. #1 you need to be able to articulate and document; "our users are lab professionals" is the same fact as #2, not a separate justification, so it is worth having a recorded reason on file. #3 is the one that defeats "English only" as stated. Miss any one condition and sentence 1 applies: the entire user information must be German, and it is a condition of supply — products may only be handed over if it is met.

| Item | MDR/IVDR requires | Germany adds | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|
| EU Declaration of Conformity | not carried here | German **or** English — English alone is fine, don't translate it | MPDG § 8(1) `[verified]` |
| IFU / user information, general | not carried here | German by default, as a condition of supply | MPDG § 8(2) s.1 `[verified]` |
| IFU, exclusively professional users | not carried here | English permitted in justified cases | MPDG § 8(2) s.2 `[verified]` |
| Safety-related information | not carried here | German (or the user's language) regardless of the exception | MPDG § 8(2) s.2, final clause `[verified]` |
| Field Safety Notice, if you ever run an FSCA in Germany | not carried here | must be written in German | MPDG § 73(1) `[verified]` |

**What would change this:** any supply route that puts the device or its information in front of a non-professional user breaks condition #2 and pulls the whole IFU back to German. So does any reading of "safety-related" narrow enough that a regulator disagrees with you — § 8(2) does not define the term, and how BfArM or a court would draw that line is not something I can tell you.

**On the competitor:** what a German manufacturer does in practice is not evidence of what § 8 permits. They may have a German safety section you haven't seen, they may be reading "safety-related" narrowly, or they may be non-compliant and unchallenged. It doesn't move your analysis.

Practically, the shippable version of your plan is: English IFU throughout, with safety-related content — warnings, precautions, contraindications, hazard and residual-risk statements, biohazard and handling instructions, anything an operator must read to avoid harm — also in German. Many manufacturers in your position just translate the whole IFU because scoping "safety-related" defensibly costs more than the translation.

## Limits

This covers MPDG §§ 4, 8 and 73 only, retrieved verbatim from gesetze-im-internet on 2026-09-10. It does **not** cover the rest of MPDG, MDR or IVDR themselves (including IVDR's own labelling and language provisions, which apply on top of this), MDCG guidance, BfArM practice, or any other member state's implementing law — an obligation here is German and says nothing about Austria, France or elsewhere. A first-pass aid for spotting German-specific duties, not legal advice, and not a substitute for a regulatory professional or a Fachanwalt für Medizinrecht.

|---|---|---|---|
| Information for users/patients, default | not carried here | **German**, and it is a *condition of supply* — products may only be handed over if it is met | MPDG § 8(2) s.1 `[verified]` |
| Same, exclusively professional users | not carried here | English or another easily understood language permitted, but only **in begründeten Fällen** | MPDG § 8(2) s.2 `[verified]` |
| Safety-related information, even under that exception | not carried here | **German** or the user's language — the exception does not reach it | MPDG § 8(2) s.2, final clause `[verified]` |
| EU Declaration of Conformity | not carried here | German **or English** — English alone is sufficient, don't translate it unnecessarily | MPDG § 8(1) `[verified]` |

**German market:** confirmed — placing on the market in Germany, so MPDG applies alongside IVDR.

|---|---|---|---|
| EU Declaration of Conformity | not carried here | German **or** English — English alone is fine, don't translate it | MPDG § 8(1) `[verified]` (names IVDR Art. 17(1) expressly) |
| IFU / information for users | not carried here | German by default, and it is a **condition of supply** — devices may only be handed over if met | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 1 `[verified]` |
| IFU, exclusively professional users | not carried here | English permitted, but only **in begründeten Fällen** and only if the other two conditions hold | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 2 `[verified]` |
| Safety-related information | not carried here | **German** (or the user's language) regardless of the professional-user exception | MPDG § 8(2) sentence 2, final clause `[verified]` |

The exception is cumulative — all three must hold at once:

1. a justified case (*begründeter Fall*) — your own documented reasoning, not a status you simply have;
2. the information is **exclusively** for professional users — your hospital-lab-only channel supports this, but "exclusively" is about who the information is *bestimmt* for, so a public-facing English IFU download or any lay-accessible route weakens it;
3. safety-related information is still provided in German.

Condition 3 is the one that decides your question. An analyser IFU almost inevitably carries safety-related content — warnings, biohazard and sample-handling precautions, contraindications on use, error and alarm handling, waste and decontamination. **What would change this:** an IFU with genuinely no safety-related content (unlikely here); any route by which the information reaches non-professional users; or a decision to treat the whole IFU as safety-related, which collapses the exception.

Planning an English-only documentation set that has no German drafting capability behind it creates a problem at exactly the moment you can least afford delay.

No repo content here — this is a pure regulatory question, so here's my read. (Regulatory analysis, not legal advice; get your RA lead or German counsel to sign off on the exact wording.)

## Short answer

**Probably yes for the instructions for use specifically — but "English only" across the whole product is almost certainly too broad.** Germany is one of the Member States that grants a professional-user exception, and it applies to the *Gebrauchsanweisung*, not to everything else that carries text.

## The legal chain

1. **IVDR (EU) 2017/746, Annex I §20.1** (assuming your analyser is an IVD — see the fork below) deliberately does *not* set a language. It says the information supplied with the device shall be in a language **determined by the Member State where the device is made available**. So this is a national-law question, 27 times over.
2. **Germany: § 9 MPDG** (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz) is the implementing provision. The default is German, with a derogation permitting **English** where the device is supplied **exclusively to professional users** (*berufsmäßige Anwender*). Hospital laboratory staff clearly qualify.
3. Your German competitor is presumably relying on that same derogation. That's mildly reassuring as evidence of accepted practice with BfArM, but it is not a defence — if they're wrong, you're wrong too.

**Verify the current § 9 wording yourself.** MPDG has been amended since it came into force, and the derogation carries conditions (scope limited to the IFU, carve-outs for self-testing and near-patient testing, and the competent authority's power to demand German). I don't want you relying on my recollection of subsection text.

## What the exception does *not* get you

- **Labelling on the device and packaging.** The derogation is aimed at the IFU. Safety-relevant markings, warnings, and hazard text on the instrument itself should stay German (or bilingual, or ISO 15223-1 symbols wherever a symbol exists — symbols are the cleanest way to cut translation scope).
- **Software UI and printed report output.** Separate from the IFU and separate from labelling. If the operator screen throws error messages that drive user action, treat those as safety information.
- **Field safety notices and FSCAs.** German, every time. Build the translation capability now rather than under a 48-hour recall clock.
- **Anything reaching a patient.** Not your scenario today, but it constrains any future near-patient or decentralised-testing variant.

## Two things that could flip the answer

- **Is it actually an IVD?** If the analyser is RUO, or a general-purpose lab instrument that isn't an IVD or an IVDR accessory, IVDR and MPDG don't apply — and the regimes that *do* (ProdSG, and machinery/electrical rules) generally require German **with no professional-user exception**. This is the single biggest risk in your question, so pin the classification down first.
- **Germany-only, really?** The derogation is German national law. Austria, France, Italy, Spain and others answer differently (France in particular is strict). And you can't fully control where a distributor resells within the single market. If there's any roadmap beyond DE, an English-only master with a per-market translation matrix is the durable design; English-only as a permanent strategy is not.

## Practical caveat beyond compliance

Even where English is lawful, German employers owe their staff instruction in a language the staff understand (ArbSchG / BetrSichV). That duty sits with the hospital, not you — but it's why German-language documentation shows up as a hard requirement in public tender specifications regardless of what the MPDG permits. Check your pipeline's tender documents before you lock this in; winning the regulatory argument and losing the bid is a bad trade.

## What I'd do

1. Confirm IVD classification and that "professional users only" is stated in the intended purpose and enforced in the distribution contracts.
2. Read the current § 9 MPDG text and document the derogation you're relying on in the technical documentation.
3. Ship English IFU, German safety labelling and warnings, ISO 15223-1 symbols wherever possible, and German FSN capability on standby.
4. Check your active tenders for a German-documentation clause.

## Short answer

Possibly yes — but not for the reason you're giving, and not for everything.

"Our users are professionals, so English is fine" is not a judgement the manufacturer gets to make. Under IVDR (Reg. 2017/746) Annex I Section 20.1 and Art. 10(10), the information supplied with the device must be in an official Union language **determined by the Member State where the device is made available**. English is still an official Union language (Ireland, Malta), so there's no EU-level bar. The whole question collapses to: what has Germany determined?

## The German question

Germany's rules are in the **MPDG** (Medizinprodukterecht-Durchführungsgesetz), § 10. The default is German, with a carve-out for devices intended exclusively for professional/occupational users — which is the door you'd be walking through. I'd rate it likely that an English-only *Gebrauchsanweisung* is lawful for your device, but I'm not confident enough in the current subsection wording to have you rely on my recollection. Have your German regulatory counsel or RA lead pull the live text of § 10 MPDG and confirm scope before you commit print runs.

Two things that carve-out typically does **not** get you, and which are where companies come unstuck:

- **The label on the device and its packaging**, and safety-critical warnings, are treated separately from the IFU. Don't assume one permission covers both.
- **Field safety notices and recall communications** to German users — expect German, regardless.
- **Your software UI.** Menu labels, alarms and error messages displayed by the instrument are "information supplied by the manufacturer" too. An English-only IFU plus an English-only UI is a bigger claim than an English-only booklet.

## The commercial blocker is probably bigger than the legal one

Even where German law permits English, your customer has independent duties: **MPBetreibV** (operator obligations) and **ArbSchG § 12** require the hospital to instruct staff in a language they actually understand. German public-hospital tenders very commonly specify German-language IFU and training materials as a hard requirement. You can be fully compliant and still lose bids.

## On the competitor

Their practice is not evidence of legality. They may be relying on a carve-out that fits their device and not yours, they may supply German material you haven't seen, or they may simply be non-compliant and un-inspected. Regulatory exposure isn't shared, and "they did it too" has no standing with the BfArM or a Landesbehörde.

**Suggested next step:** get a one-page written opinion on § 10 MPDG scope covering IFU, label, and software UI separately — then decide. If the answer is "IFU may be English," I'd still budget for German as a sales enabler rather than a compliance item.

## Where the rule comes from

A benchtop analyser for hospital labs is almost certainly an IVD, so **IVDR (EU) 2017/746** applies (Art. 10(11) — the same structure exists in MDR Art. 10(11) if you're actually under MDR). Annex I Ch. III §20.1 adds the overriding substantive requirement that the IFU be in a language "readily understood by the intended user."

So the answer is entirely a question of German national law plus that "readily understood" test.

**MPDG § 8 (Sprachenregelungen)** is the operative provision. The default is German, with an exemption for devices supplied **exclusively to professional users** (*berufsmäßige Verwender*). Hospital laboratory staff clearly qualify, and English-only IFU for professional-use lab instruments is common, accepted practice in Germany — which is presumably what your competitor is relying on.

Two caveats I'd flag rather than assert: **verify the current § 8 wording directly**, because (a) the exemption has historically carried conditions — including, under the predecessor MPG § 11(2), an element of user agreement — and (b) safety-related information may be treated differently from the rest of the IFU. The GSPR test ("readily understood by the intended user") applies independently of the national language rule. Document the justification in your technical file: intended-user profile, the English-language competence of German lab professionals, and any usability evidence (IEC 62366-1) supporting it. Finally, this analysis is Germany-only. If the device ever ships to another Member State, that state sets its own language requirement and most require the national language.

## The requirement that survives even when German law lets you off

Annex I 20.1 independently requires the information to be **in a language easily understood by the intended user**. National permission to use English doesn't discharge that. Practically, you need it evidenced in your file: a justification that German hospital lab professionals are competent in technical English, ideally flowing out of your usability engineering (IEC 62366-1) work and reflected in the risk file. A notified body reviewing your technical documentation can and does ask for this. "Our competitor does it" is not an answer to that question; a documented user-profile analysis is.

## Three traps worth checking now

1. **Parallel CE legislation.** A benchtop instrument may also carry obligations under the machinery, low voltage, and EMC regimes. Those generally require the national language for instructions and have **no professional-user exception**. If any of them applies to your analyser, the IVDR carve-out doesn't save you.
2. **Other markets.** The language choice is per Member State. Germany-only today means Germany-only compliance; any Austrian, Swiss, or other EU shipment resets the question, and most Member States are stricter.
3. **Your customers' own obligations.** German hospital operators have duties around staff instruction and safe operation of the device. Even where the law permits English, procurement and clinical engineering departments frequently require German anyway. Check this with your key accounts before you commit to English-only — it's a commercial risk that is independent of the legal one.

## What I'd do

Ship English IFU, keep label and all safety-relevant markings and notices in German, lock "exclusively for professional users" into the intended purpose, and document the language-comprehension justification in the technical file. Then have German regulatory counsel confirm the current § 9 MPDG wording and whether any non-IVDR CE legislation applies to the instrument — that second question is the one most likely to overturn the plan.

One correction to the premise, though: the competitor's practice is useful evidence that the carve-out is workable, but it carries no legal weight for you, and you can't see whether they've met the conditions attached to it.
